group.passage:
Insurance against disaster at sea is much older than the coffee house that made it famous. By the sixteenth century, English merchants were already agreeing, for a fee, to pay part of the loss if a ship or its cargo went down. Most did this only as a side business to their main trade, and the fee depended on the distance, the dangers of the sea and the risk from enemies. What London lacked was a dependable place where people seeking such protection could meet people willing to offer it.
Coffee houses soon filled that gap. In the late 1600s they served as offices, mailboxes and news centers for men of business, and each tended to attract its own crowd. The earliest known record of Edward Lloyd's coffee house is not a business notice at all but a newspaper advertisement from 1689 about some stolen watches. In 1691 Lloyd moved to Lombard Street, in the heart of the city's trade, where merchants, ship owners and sea captains gathered to buy ships at auction and exchange news. He even printed his own newspaper, Lloyd's News, three times a week.
Yet there is no sign that Lloyd himself took a special interest in insurance, and when he died in 1713, nothing linked his house more closely to insurance than to any other kind of trade. Its future was decided by a law passed seven years later. Parliament allowed two new companies to insure ships and banned every other company or partnership from doing so. Private individuals, however, could still insure ships on their own. Unable to join together as firms, these individual insurers needed a common meeting place, and Lloyd's, with its steady supply of shipping news, became their home. In 1734 the house began publishing Lloyd's List, largely because the insurers wanted reliable reports on ships.
The coffee house itself did not last. By the 1760s, gamblers placing bets disguised as insurance had crowded in, and in 1769 many serious insurers left to set up a New Lloyd's nearby. In 1774 they moved into rooms at the Royal Exchange, carrying with them the name of a coffee-house keeper who had never set out to build an insurance market.

translation_zh.text:
海上災難的保險，比讓它出名的那家咖啡館古老得多。到了十六世紀，英國商人就已經會收取一筆費用，答應在船隻或貨物沉沒時賠償部分損失。大多數人只把這當成本業之外的副業，而費用的高低取決於航程遠近、海上的危險和遭遇敵人的風險。倫敦缺的是一個可靠的地方，讓需要這種保障的人和願意提供保障的人碰面。
咖啡館很快就填補了這個空缺。十七世紀後期，咖啡館是生意人的辦公室、信箱和新聞中心，而每家咖啡館往往吸引自己的一群客人。目前所知最早提到愛德華‧洛伊德（Edward Lloyd）咖啡館的紀錄，根本不是商業啟事，而是 1689 年一則關於幾支失竊手錶的報紙廣告。1691 年，洛伊德搬到倫敦商業中心的倫巴底街，商人、船東和船長聚集在那裡拍賣買船、交換消息。他甚至自己印報紙《洛伊德新聞》，每週出刊三次。
然而，沒有跡象顯示洛伊德本人對保險特別有興趣；1713 年他過世時，他的咖啡館與保險的關係，並不比與其他任何行業更密切。決定它未來的，是七年後通過的一條法律。國會准許兩家新公司承保船隻，並禁止其他所有公司或合夥經營者承保。不過，個人仍然可以自己承保船隻。這些個人保險業者無法合組公司，需要一個共同的聚會地點，而擁有穩定航運消息的洛伊德咖啡館就成了他們的據點。1734 年，這家咖啡館開始發行《洛伊德船舶日報》，主要是因為保險業者想要可靠的船隻消息。
咖啡館本身並沒有延續下去。到了 1760 年代，用保險當幌子下注的賭客擠了進來；1769 年，許多正派的保險業者離開，在附近另立「新洛伊德」。1774 年，他們搬進皇家交易所的房間，一併帶走的，是一位從沒想過要建立保險市場的咖啡館老闆的名字。
